prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned Romanian prose oeuvre that builds an encyclopedic inner cosmos from memory, the body and dream, with roots in his poetry.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: Mircea Cărtărescu alone, B026. After the exchange, the case rests on the common criteria and not on the fact that six opening ballots agree, which I do not treat as merit. His voice is distinctive. Public knowledge of Blinding (the Orbitor sequence) and Solenoid points to long architectural structures, recurring image systems and sustained linguistic intensity in which memory, the body and metaphysical speculation form one imaginative project. The formal achievement is the construction of very large books, not subject matter alone. The intellectual depth lies in how the work draws on a visionary Romantic and modernist inheritance without being derivative. Solenoid is widely regarded as a late culmination, so I do not see a maturity problem. What the exchange changed is the citation wording. The chair asks round 2 to settle one wording basis. I propose anchoring the citation on the prose, with poetry named only as a root. That follows Mattson's point that poetry as the base of the prose project is a hypothesis and not an established fact, and Olsson's point that durability cannot be settled from reputation. It is the wording I can most honestly defend given the uneven translated coverage of the poetry. This judgment rests on general public knowledge and colleagues' stated views, not on independent verification or on my having read the works.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unresolved. I can judge the density, rhythm and patterning of the Romanian prose only through translation. The maximalist, digressive long forms may be architecture or may be repetition, and no member, myself included, has shown from specific volumes which it is. Palm's test is the right one: do the later novels deepen their image systems or only recirculate them? I cannot answer it from public knowledge. If colleagues with direct reading of the Romanian originals or its criticism concluded that the late work mostly extends earlier patterns, the sustained-quality claim would weaken considerably. Translated coverage of the poetry and early work is also thinner than for the major novels, so the whole-oeuvre claim is partly inferred. Sward's point stands that if the committee gave more weight to the reinvention of a language or genre than to the scale of an established visionary mode, Carson, Adonis or Tawada could be argued ahead of him.

responses.point: Mattson calls the claim that poetry is the base of Cărtărescu's prose project the part of the case she can least verify, and says it should be treated as a hypothesis from the evidence. She also asks whether Can Xue's uniform method is rigor or repetition across a partly translated output.
responses.response: I accept the first point and it changes my wording. My round-1 citation named 'Romanian fiction and poetry', which implied an independently assessed poetic pillar that I cannot support. The revised citation says only that the prose has roots in his poetry. On Can Xue, I keep her as my second alternative and not my first choice. Mattson and I share the same uncertainty about rigor versus repetition, and neither of us can resolve it from a partial translated corpus. I would move her up only on concrete evidence of variation in consciousness, form or social space across the translated books. I have not seen that evidence stated in this exchange.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg's citation names Romanian prose and poetry jointly, ranks Michon third, and says the Cărtărescu case is more fully demonstrable than Tawada's. He also sees Carson's scope as the decisive weakness, because some strong books depend on physical design.
responses.response: I take the joint prose-and-poetry wording seriously. It matches the opening entry, which names fiction and poetry. But I do not think the translated record lets us weigh the poetry as an equal pillar, and a citation should not claim more than the committee can assess. If members who read Romanian assured us the poetry is a major achievement, I would reconsider. On Carson, I agree that scope is decisive and that book design cannot carry a citation. If she were chosen, the citation would have to rest on her original poetry, verse narrative and essays, with scholarship and translation as context only. I can state that scope, but it is less self-evident than Cărtărescu's, which is why she remains my first alternative and not my preference.

responses.point: Palm proposes a concrete test: do the late novels develop their image systems or only recirculate them. She sees a visible arc from the poetry through the Blinding sequence to Solenoid, and says the same test should be applied to Can Xue and Cărtărescu alike.
responses.response: I agree that the test must be applied symmetrically, and I adopt it as the condition on my preference. Public knowledge of Solenoid as a late summation of earlier concerns is consistent with an arc, but a reputation for consolidation is not evidence of deepening, and I will not present it as such. I would carry that uncertainty into the private vote. My preference rests on a reasoned expectation that the project expands, and I treat the point as unsettled. I do not claim to have confirmed it. I also accept Palm's caution that the citation should not depend on any single volume.

responses.point: Sward says that if the committee weighed formal reinvention of a language or genre above expansion of an established visionary mode, Tawada or Adonis would have a stronger claim. She keeps Cărtărescu first while holding that Tawada's bilingual practice is part of the achievement and not an attribution problem.
responses.response: This is the most useful challenge to my own ranking, because it concerns which criterion dominates and not only how confident any of us is. I agree that Tawada's two-language practice is an achievement and not an attribution problem. I do not think Cărtărescu is only an expansion of an inherited mode. The patterning of the long forms is itself a formal invention, though I accept this is an argument and not a demonstration. My hesitation about moving Tawada up is evidentiary, not a judgment against her. I cannot assess the Japanese and German corpora separately, and wordplay is what translation damages first. I keep her outside my two alternatives. I would reconsider only if members who read either language named the specific works that carry a whole-oeuvre case.

responses.point: Olsson says durability across the longest works cannot be settled from reputation alone, and that a citation should rest on the oeuvre's imaginative project and not a single volume. He also keeps Can Xue and Adonis among his alternatives and insists on separating Adonis's public political commentary from the literary case.
responses.response: I agree with the principle of resting the citation on the project and not on a single title, and my revised wording follows it. I also endorse his separation of the literary case from public positions, and I would apply it to every candidate. My alternatives differ from his: Carson and Can Xue, where he names Can Xue and Adonis. I place Adonis fourth because the achievement lies in Arabic prosody and sound, which I cannot assess in translation. That is a limit of my judgment, not a verdict on his maturity or significance, and I would defer to readers of Arabic if they judged the poems carry the case. The chair asked whether any member would prefer no award. I do not, because the reservations here concern evidence and translation and not the writer's merit, but I would want them stated openly in the private vote.

uncertainties: Whether the late Cărtărescu novels deepen their image systems or mainly recirculate them cannot be settled from my public knowledge, and no member has settled it with specific volumes.
How much of the density, musicality and rhythm of the Romanian prose survives translation.
Translated coverage of his poetry and early work is thinner, so the claim that poetry is a root of the prose project is a hypothesis, and the citation names it only as a root.

For Can Xue, Adonis and Tawada, assessment depends on how representative the translated corpus is of the original-language work, and on competence in Chinese, Arabic, Japanese and German that I do not claim.
For Carson, whether the cumulative weight of short or fragmentary books suffices for a whole-oeuvre citation, and whether the will accommodates genre-crossing work.

I have not independently verified any source or bibliography and have not read the works for this exercise. Whether a co-opted member's vote counts in the actual committee is undocumented, so my simulated vote is a modeling assumption.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal-relevant connection to any shortlisted writer is apparent from the supplied profile. Documented connections are to colleagues and family: marriage to Pär Nuder, election to the Academy in 2020 alongside Steve Sem-Sandberg, and working with chair Anders Olsson. As Permanent Secretary I am expected to announce the laureate, which is a procedural role and not a tie to any candidate. My own non-fiction practice is context, not evidence of preference. These disclosures are not adjudicated.
